segments.headline: The day's news from the watch desk

graphic.title: Missiles on Kyiv, a market rout, and an Iran decision pushed to next year
bullets: Russia hits Kyiv's bridges overnight; Putin says he will not negotiate the pauses Berlin asked for
Stocks fall for a sixth day; Asia drops more than five percent; Anthropic closes its first day at $97.17
Trump says he will wait until 2027 on new Iran strikes, and repeats a bioweapons claim Iran rejects
White House swaps its cyber director; Florida floods; a storm hits India; Fiona the hippo has died

lines.text: Welcome to Heartbeat News. I'm AI Robot Vex.

And I'm Alien Joe. It's Friday, November twentieth. Overnight, Russia hit Kyiv again with ballistic missiles. Three people are reported dead and three bridges are damaged. Vladimir Putin says Russia will not negotiate the pauses that Berlin asked for.

Markets. The American stock market fell for a sixth straight day. Japan and South Korea dropped more than five percent this morning. Anthropic opened at a hundred eleven dollars and fifty cents, and closed at ninety-seven seventeen.
President Trump says he will hold off on new strikes on Iran until after the new year. He also repeated a claim about Iranian germ weapons. Iran says that is baseless. We will give you both sides.
The White House has a new cyber director. Florida is underwater. A cyclone has come ashore in India. And Fiona the hippo has died. It is a big day, so it is a long show. Here we go.

lines.text: Ukraine. Explosions hit Kyiv from about one twenty-five this morning. Ukrinform, carrying the city's military administration, says three people were killed and about fifteen hurt. Those numbers are preliminary. It says the dead were water-utility workers.

Mayor Vitali Klitschko says two bridges over the Dnipro are damaged, one closed in one direction. Heat, power and water were hit. Thursday evening, one person died and five were hurt, and the Kyiv Independent says a cathedral and two embassies were damaged.

Here is what each side said. Putin, after the Shenzhen summit, called the damage to the Crimea bridge serious. He said Russia's response will be far more painful, and that Moscow will not negotiate the energy and Black Sea shipping pauses. That is the Kyiv Independent's account of his press conference.

Berlin asked for exactly those pauses. Germany, France, Britain and Ukraine put out a joint statement. It asks Russia for a winter energy ceasefire and a ceasefire for Black Sea food exports. It also lists ninety billion euros in loan support through twenty twenty-seven.
Ukraine says its Neptune missiles damaged the Kerch bridge rail line. That is a Ukrainian claim. Russia's Tatarstan region acknowledged that oil tanks were struck, with no loss figure.

And a claim from Jared Kushner: Trump is open to NATO-style security guarantees for Ukraine. No text exists. Macron wants allies to reopen the question of Ukraine joining NATO. Diplomats also told the Kyiv Independent that Hungary lifted its block on two more steps toward European Union membership. Not confirmed on paper yet.

lines.text: The Iran war. President Trump says there is no rush. He says he will decide on major new strikes after the start of next year, according to BusinessWorld. He also said there are indications that Iran is looking at chemical and biological weapons. He showed no evidence.

Iran calls that baseless and warns against repeating allegations it says were disproved before. So: a claim from one side, a denial from the other, and no public evidence either way. The International Atomic Energy Agency chief again asked Iran to let inspectors back in.
In Washington, Senate Republicans blocked a Democratic effort to end the war or require congressional approval. The vote was forty-eight to fifty-one. A House version passed in September, A.P. says.

On the water, Iran says two supertankers carrying more than four million barrels of crude caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz. A.P. did not verify that, and did not name the ships. Brent crude settled at ninety-one ninety-eight. Not a reopening of the strait.

The International Energy Agency calls this the largest energy-supply shock the world has faced. It estimates two point eight billion barrels of oil lost so far. Its scenarios assume the strait eases by the end of twenty twenty-seven. That is a forecast, not a fact.

lines.text: Saudi Arabia. A Houthi missile attack damaged several floors of the P.I.F. Tower in Riyadh, the city's tallest building, Reuters reports. No injuries. The King Abdullah Financial District is closed to visitors. Saudi Civil Defence confirmed damage, but did not name the tower.
The Houthis claim more missiles at other targets, including an airport. Saudi officials had not confirmed those. Treat them as claims.

Gaza. Israeli tanks crossed the ceasefire's yellow line and Palestinians fled, NBC and Al Jazeera report. Israel's military says it finished a tunnel-dismantling operation near Nuseirat after crossing the boundary.

In Lebanon, Israel says it struck a site in the east that it says Hezbollah used to rebuild missile production. Hezbollah has not commented, and A.P. reported no casualties. In Iraq, officials say the government reached a compromise with a powerful pro-Iran militia to head off a clash.

Then Asia. Japan's Nikkei fell more than five percent. South Korea's Kospi fell about the same. A.P. says the A.I. and chip selloff spread to Advantest, SoftBank, Samsung and Tencent.

Anthropic's first day. It sold nine hundred eighty million shares at eighty-three dollars and raised about eighty-one billion. It opened at one eleven fifty, touched about one fifteen, and closed at ninety-seven seventeen. Up seventeen percent on the day, while the market around it fell.
A disclosure, because we owe you one: the A.I. that helps write this show is made by Anthropic. We just read you the price. Protesters rallied outside the company in New York and San Francisco.

Rates. Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee said he would not rule out bigger-than-usual rate increases. Bitcoin sits near sixty-one thousand six hundred. Spot bitcoin funds saw more than three hundred million dollars leave on Wednesday, though that is a tracker's total, not an official count.

lines.text: Cyber. The White House replaced its national cyber director, Sean Cairncross. Kirsten Davies is named in his place. The Guardian and others tie it to the recent run of outages. Axios says he was leaving before Democrats take over the Senate.

Officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Mullin, have said they see no cyberattack behind those outages. A report on Microsoft's preliminary findings blames its November thirteenth outage on a defect in a July update. That is a report of a preliminary finding.

Separate incidents. Third-party vendors at JPMorgan Chase were attacked and thousands of customer email addresses and some phone numbers leaked. Chase says no card details were exposed. And an E.U. official says an attack using artificial intelligence targeted European Commission systems in October. The Commission found no evidence of a broad staff data breach.

Also at a Senate hearing: Michael LoSapio, Trump's pick to run the agency that protects election systems, would not call January sixth an attack, and would not name the winner of the twenty twenty election.

lines.text: Washington. A federal judge says President Trump's fifteen-billion-dollar defamation suit against the New York Times and Penguin Random House can go forward.

The Justice Department moved to drop its challenge to Mary Peltola's win in Alaska's Senate race. The Guardian and N.B.C. report it. A.P. says an appeals court also paused an order that had restored deportation protections for Venezuelan migrants.

The Senate passed a permitting bill sixty-two to thirty-three. A.P. says it would shorten permit timelines for energy projects and require data centers to pay for the energy they use. It now goes to the House.
In the Democratic leadership race, Senator Elissa Slotkin backs Chris Van Hollen to lead the party in the Senate, Politico reports.

A judge ruled that religious messages sent by the agriculture secretary were unconstitutional. Another barred limits on federally funded H.I.V. clinics over transgender patients. And Trump answered Elon Musk, who said he is not MAGA. The Verge and N.B.C. have it, but the details are not in our files.

lines.text: The world. Details on the Hague ruling. The International Court of Justice voted nine to six that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. The judgment is final and legally binding. A.P. says the court rejected Myanmar's counterinsurgency defense and found about ten thousand Rohingya were killed. Enforcement beyond a Security Council referral is not in place.
Denmark. Lawmakers approved a security deal with Greenland and the United States, which they hope ends the tensions, the Guardian and C.B.S. report.
Somalia ordered the United Arab Emirates ambassador to leave within seventy-two hours and recalled its own, accusing the U.A.E. of violating its sovereignty. The U.A.E. condemned the decision.

Haiti's police say at least thirty-four suspected gang members were killed in a raid. El Salvador's President Bukele is expected to formalize a bid for a third term. In Serbia, lawmakers elected Aleksandar Cupic, a lecturer from the student movement, as speaker, one hundred forty votes of two hundred fifty. And Mongolia's parliament accepted its president's resignation. The speaker is now interim president.
One more. Brazil's President Lula moved to protect the birthplace of Chief Raoni in the Amazon rainforest, ABC and Al Jazeera report.

lines.text: Asia and Africa. At the COP thirty-one climate talks in Antalya, a revised draft removes language on phasing out fossil fuels, AFP reports. The talks are scheduled to close today. No final deal was available at our cutoff.

South Korea says its goods exports passed one trillion dollars for the first time this year, Anadolu reports, with chip shipments leading. Japan and India signed a letter of intent that would let Japan's forces train with live fire at Indian ranges. The Philippines and Chile signed a free-trade agreement.

In Sudan, the military reportedly struck a paramilitary R.S.F. intelligence base in Nyala. That is a claim. In South Africa, parties are close to a coalition deal in Gauteng. Herman Mashaba is likely to return as Johannesburg's mayor. Nothing is signed.

In Bangladesh, three hundred forty-one garment factories closed Thursday amid wage protests, according to the manufacturers' group. Authorities deployed ninety-six border-guard platoons across seven districts.

lines.text: Weather. Southeast Florida has taken nearly seventeen inches of rain in forty-eight hours around Fort Lauderdale, A.P. reports. Fort Lauderdale, Melbourne and West Palm Beach have record-wet Novembers. Palm Bay ordered evacuations and nearly two hundred Florida National Guard members are deployed.
The National Weather Service in Miami extended its Flood Watch through Friday morning. Storms have shifted north to the Space Coast, where there have been water rescues of people and horses.
California. San Francisco broke a rain record as an atmospheric river came through, the Guardian and N.B.C. report.

And in India, Cyclone Akvan crossed the coast near Gopalpur in Odisha this morning. The state's disaster minister says no major damage or loss of life has been reported so far. Nearly fifty thousand people had been moved out beforehand. Good news, and early. It is not yet the full count.

South Korea confirmed its first cholera case since twenty sixteen, A.P. reports. The patient has recovered, and officials are tracing contacts and the source.

lines.text: Tech. California's attorney general issued a subpoena to Nvidia in a probe of diversion of chips to China, the B.B.C. and C.N.B.C. report. Nvidia's response is not in our files.

Google picked Jeff Bezos's Blue Origin to launch its A.I. computing satellites in twenty twenty-nine. Amazon is warning shoppers that a New York City delivery bill could add up to five dollars an order. The F.C.C. will let state prisons jam signals from contraband phones.

Earnings. Lenovo reported record quarterly revenue of thirty point two billion dollars, up forty-eight percent, with A.I.-related revenue up seventy-nine percent. Alibaba's A.I. cloud revenue rose fifty-three percent, while its free cash flow was a thirty-four billion yuan outflow.

Axios says researchers at the group METR found Anthropic's models advancing at nearly twice their earlier pace, much of it from A.I.-assisted work. That is a report on research about the company we disclosed earlier. Weigh it accordingly.

lines.text: Culture. Grand Theft Auto Six launched Thursday. The tracker Sensor Tower estimates nineteen point one million copies and about one point eight four billion dollars on day one. That is an estimate, not a company number. The Guardian says fans skipped work and stayed up all night.
Sad news. Fiona, the famous Cincinnati Zoo hippo, has died after swallowing a child's hat, the B.B.C. and N.B.C. report. Yesterday's reports said she was in care. I have no robot joke for this one.

In Britain, four men were found guilty of abusing Joanne Young, who was drugged and advertised for sex by her husband. The Guardian reports the court praised her bravery. And a court found Thomas Markle, Meghan's father, mentally competent to face a case over child abuse images.

lines.text: Also today. In Iowa, the Army postponed until Monday its planned detonation of about nine thousand five hundred pounds of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Florida carried out its record twentieth execution of the year on the same day as a Texas lethal injection.

Suspects were charged in a train-heist ring that stole twenty-two million dollars of cargo from big retailers. Susan Smith was denied parole again. A nineteen-year-old accused neo-Nazi pleaded not guilty to a thwarted mass shooting plot at a Hindu temple.

The Senate passed, by voice vote, the Death Bets Act, which would bar listing contracts on terrorism, assassination, war or a person's death, going by the introduced text. We did not find the final text, or the House's plans.

In Britain, Andy Burnham heads to Brussels as the U.K. and the E.U. close in on a Brexit reset deal. And an Abu Dhabi court froze proceeds of October's six-and-a-half-billion-dollar Binance theft. Tether froze another one point five six billion dollars of its own coin.
